explanation: The Four Seasons is a set of four violin concertos, each in three movements. Holst's suite has seven, one for each planet known in his day except Earth.

claims.text: Vivaldi's The Four Seasons consists of four violin concertos, each in three movements, 12 movements in all.
Holst's The Planets has seven movements.
Holst's seven movements are named after the planets known in his day other than Earth.

issues.note: Explanation and c3 say 'known in his day'. Pluto was found in 1930, four years before Holst died, so a pedant could read 'in his day' as including it. 'one for each planet known when he wrote it, except Earth' would be exact. True under the natural reading, so a note only.

evidence.restatement: Vivaldi's The Four Seasons is four violin concertos of three movements each, so 12 movements.

claimResults.note: Rival test: someone may expect four movements, one per season; the work is a set of concertos.

claimResults.note: Colin Matthews's 2000 'Pluto' addition is not Holst's and would still leave 8 against 12.

evidence.restatement: Holst's seven movements are Mars, Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, the planets known in his day other than Earth.

editor.reason: Both checks pass, but high-risk claims c1 (number), c2 (number) and c3 (number) rest on knowledge only: neither check carries dataset or web evidence (A's records say WebSearch was unavailable, B ran no search) and no pinned dataset covers these music facts, so §9.9 rule 3 cannot pass. No wording fix adds evidence, and stepping down the precision ladder changes claims (§9.2), so it is cut. The content read as sound; redraft under a new id with web evidence or without the risky detail. For the redraft, A's note stands: 'known in his day' should read 'known when he wrote it', since Pluto was found in 1930, before Holst died.
